# The canonical register: Karma

*A letter to a colleague, 31 July 2026 — on the name Karma, and on the forms that keep failing it.*

Your note said, roughly: surely the marks are a nicety. Permit me to use Karma to show they are not.

First, the attestation. The attested form is **कर्म**, from the tradition's own record. The canonical transliteration is **Karma**.

Say it aloud as the sources heard it: “KAHR-muh” The marks are what carry that sound to a reader who has never heard it spoken.

On the plain form — and I want to be precise, because you pushed on this. The plain form *karma* differs from the canonical *Karma* only by convention of display — case, not content. It is *acceptable everywhere*: in legacy systems, in plain-text citation, in the DNS itself. What is not acceptable is what follows in the register: respellings that change the letters, not just their case.

One more thing, because it always surprises: the name did not stay home. Karma is the one doctrine shared by Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain without alteration of name — the subcontinent’s common physics.  The West received it through theosophy and thence into the global vernacular, where ‘karma’ now means cosmic payback in any language; classical comparisons run to the Egyptian heart-weighing and the Greek Adrasteia.

And it never stopped working. The word entered every major language as a loan — among the few Sanskrit terms to do so.  It underwrites the theory of rebirth, the ethics of non-harm (the deed’s victim returns as one’s debtor), and the quietist strand of Indian political thought: the revolution you cannot make today, your karma will make eventually.

## The Convention's Own History

Long before IAST was formalized in 1912, Sanskrit had Pāṇini — the fourth-century-BCE grammarian whose rules describe the language's sounds with a precision no other ancient tradition matched. That heritage is why the convention is so exact: retroflexes (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ) are not accented dentals but separate phonemes with separate meanings; long and short vowels (ā/a, ī/i, ū/u) change words, not just timing. IAST writes those distinctions down with underdots and macrons so that a reader who has never heard Sanskrit can still read it *correctly*. Dropping the marks is not transliteration at a lower resolution — it is a different, lesser claim.

## The Address, Without an Encoding Detour

The canonical form **Karma** already uses ordinary Latin letters, so the address bar needs no special encoding narrative. The digital temple can preserve the spelling exactly as the scholarly record presents it. That is the practical point here: consistency between the source, the citation, and the public address.

This does not make every romanization equally valid. A wrong letter remains wrong even when it is easy to type. Canonical status still depends on the attested convention, never on convenience or registrar inventory.

Write back when you have checked the sources; they are better company than I am.

*— The Register*

## The Verdict

**Karma** is the canonical form: attested, checkable, and enforced across the temple, the lexicon, the cards, the APIs, and this register. The plain form *karma* shares that standing — the two are the same name in every system. The false forms above are documented so that no reader has to take the temple's word on faith — the violations are stated, the sources are named, and the register stands open to challenge on every line.

The temple of **Karma** stands at [/karma/](/karma/).

The docket for this ruling: no false forms on the docket; no contested forms attested; the attestation rests on 4 cited sources — Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.2.13, Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.292 (deeds and intention), Mahābhārata, Savitrī episode.
